hook.text: Here's the whole job of a language model. It takes a sequence of tokens, and gives back a probability for every token that could come next.

vocab.text: Not one word. A score for every token in its vocabulary, and this one has two hundred thousand.

pick.text: Picking one is a separate step... and how it picks is a knob you control.

loop.text: To write, it picks a token, adds it to the end, and runs again on the longer input.

again.text: The, cat, sat, on, the, mat, and then a token that means done.

plan.text: Notice what's missing from that loop: a plan. The sentence shows up because each step was reasonable, not because anything decided it in advance.

weights.text: There's no database, either. What it knows lives in its weights, numbers tuned in training until its guesses matched real text.

same.text: That's why a well known fact and an invented citation come out of the same machinery, and sound just as sure.

token-in.text: So what is a token, exactly?

token.text: It's a chunk of text that the vocabulary gives a single number, called its id. Sometimes a whole word, often just a piece.

straw.text: Take strawberry. On its own, GPT-4o's tokenizer cuts it in three: ess-tee, raw, berry.

ids.text: And the model gets three ids: three oh two, sixteen eighteen, nineteen seven seven two.

space.text: Put a space in front, the way it sits inside a sentence, and the whole word is one id.

letters.text: [curious] So how many R's are in strawberry? The model never saw the letters. It has to recall facts about the spelling, instead of looking.

rate.text: For English, the rule of thumb is about four characters a token, or three quarters of a word. So a thousand tokens is roughly seven hundred and fifty words.

newer.text: Newer tokenizers often do better. This one turns the lesson's opening, a hundred and ninety characters, into thirty-six tokens.

bpe-in.text: But who decided where strawberry gets cut? Nobody did. The vocabulary was learned.

bpe.text: The usual way is called byte pair encoding, or BPE, and you can run it by hand.

corpus.text: Here's a tiny training text. Low, five times. Lower, twice. Newest, three times. And widest, twice.

split.text: Split every word into characters, with a marker for where the word ends.

count.text: Now count every pair of neighbours. L and O sit side by side seven times, and so do O and W.

merge.text: Merge the most frequent pair into one new symbol, write the merge down, and count again.

order.text: L and O first. Then that with W, making low. Then low at the end of a word.

suffix.text: Then E and S, then T, then the word end. Nobody told it about suffixes. Est ends both newest and widest, so it earned its merges early.

after.text: After ten merges, low and newest are single tokens. Widest is still four pieces, because wid never came up often enough.

list.text: And that list of merges is the tokenizer. New text gets split into characters, and the merges are replayed in order.

rule.text: Frequent text ends up as cheap, whole tokens. Rare text stays in pieces.

counts-in.text: And the pieces are what you pay for.

bytes.text: Underneath every token there are bytes. An English letter is one byte. A Japanese or Hindi character is three.

hello.text: This tokenizer starts from bytes, and merges what it saw often. Hello in Japanese is fifteen bytes, and just one token. In Hindi, eighteen bytes make four.

azul.text: But in Tifinagh, a Berber script it rarely saw, hello is twelve bytes... and twelve tokens.

formats.text: What the text is matters too. The lesson's prose sample runs four and a half characters a token. Its Python, under two and a half.

json.text: Three records cost eighty-nine tokens as JSON, but thirty-three as CSV, because JSON repeats every key on every record.

models.text: And every model family has its own tokenizer. GPT-3's counts that same JSON as a hundred and twenty. Anthropic says its newest one makes about thirty percent more tokens of the same text than the last.

price.text: So a model that's twenty percent cheaper per token, but counts thirty percent more tokens, costs you about four percent more.

chat.text: One more trap. A chat resends its whole history on every turn.

turns.text: In the lesson's example, ten turns build a conversation seven thousand tokens long. But you're billed for forty-three thousand five hundred input tokens... over six times its length.

number.text: And each of those tokens reaches the model as an id, which is just a number.

next.text: Nothing in nineteen seven seven two says berry is anything like cherry.
